title: We Asked Vogue, GQ, and a Pro Stylist to Kill Jensen Huang’s Leather Jacket

sections.title: Conversation 1
sections.scene: Two colleagues discuss a news story about a tech CEO's fashion choices and its public-relations implications.

script.en: Did you see that article about Jensen Huang's leather jacket? It seems like everyone on social media is talking about it.
I did. It's strange how a single piece of clothing can trigger so much discussion. But I suppose when you're the CEO of a company worth over a trillion dollars, everything you do gets scrutinized.
Exactly. The article suggested that his new look—those tight leather jackets—sends the wrong message. They quoted a stylist saying it makes him look like he's going through a midlife crisis.
I'm not sure I agree. I mean, isn't it his personal choice? Why should the public care what he wears?
Well, the argument is that his image affects investor confidence. If he looks like he's not taking his role seriously, people might start to question his judgment.
That seems like a stretch. Investors care about profits, not fashion. But I do think the timing is unfortunate—he's been in the news for other reasons lately.
You mean the rumors about his personal life? The article didn't mention that, but it did say his wife actually picks out his clothes because he finds most fabrics uncomfortable.
That's interesting. So maybe he's not trying to make a fashion statement at all. He just wears what his wife tells him to. That changes the whole narrative.
Right. And the stylists they interviewed suggested he should switch to something more understated—like a simple Oxford shirt and a crewneck sweater. They think it would make him look more serious.
I can see that. But honestly, I think this whole discussion is a distraction. We should be focusing on the company's performance, not the CEO's wardrobe.

script.en: In recent years, the public image of technology executives has undergone a noticeable transformation. Once content to be seen in casual hoodies and jeans, many now embrace high-end fashion, hiring personal stylists and appearing at fashion shows. This shift is not merely personal; it reflects a broader effort to reshape the public's perception of the tech industry itself. According to fashion insiders, tech leaders are increasingly aware that their appearance can influence how they are perceived by investors, employees, and the general public. A polished look may convey competence and seriousness, while an overly casual or eccentric style could undermine credibility. As a result, some executives have turned to professional stylists for guidance. However, not everyone welcomes this trend. Critics argue that focusing on fashion distracts from more substantive issues, such as ethical concerns and corporate governance. They contend that the public should judge leaders by their actions and decisions, not by their clothing. also, excessive attention to appearance may reinforce superficial values in the business world. Interestingly, the debate over executive fashion often reveals deeper anxieties about the role of technology in society. When a tech leader adopts a dramatic new look, it can symbolize a break from the industry's traditional roots, raising questions about whether success has led to a loss of authenticity. The conversation about clothing thus becomes a proxy for broader discussions about power, responsibility, and identity. in the end, whether one approves or disapproves, the scrutiny of tech executives' wardrobes shows no sign of fading. In an age where image is constantly curated and shared, the line between personal choice and public expectation remains blurred. What matters most, perhaps, is that the attention does not overshadow the real issues that technology companies and their leaders must address.

sections.title: The Fashion Makeover of Tech Executives
sections.passage: In recent years, the public image of technology executives has undergone a striking transformation that few could have anticipated a decade ago. Once content to be seen in casual hoodies and jeans, many now embrace high-end fashion, hiring personal stylists and appearing at fashion shows alongside celebrities and designers. This shift is not merely personal; it reflects a broader effort to reshape the public's perception of the tech industry itself, which has increasingly come under scrutiny for its growing power and influence in society. According to fashion insiders, tech leaders are increasingly aware that their appearance can influence how they are perceived by investors, employees, and the general public. A polished look may convey competence and seriousness, while an overly casual or eccentric style could undermine credibility in settings where major financial decisions are made. As a result, some executives have turned to professional stylists for guidance on how to present themselves in public. For instance, a CEO's decision to wear a tailored suit instead of a hoodie can signal a new level of professionalism and a willingness to be taken seriously by traditional business partners. However, not everyone welcomes this trend, and some observers remain deeply skeptical of its implications. Critics argue that focusing on fashion distracts from more substantive issues, such as ethical concerns and corporate governance, which deserve far greater attention from both the media and the public. They contend that the public should judge leaders by their actions and decisions, not by their clothing, and that style should never become a substitute for substance. also, excessive attention to appearance may reinforce superficial values in the business world, where substance should matter more than style in shaping long-term reputations. Interestingly, the debate over executive fashion often reveals deeper anxieties about the role of technology in society and the people who lead it. When a tech leader adopts a dramatic new look, it can symbolize a break from the industry's traditional roots, raising questions about whether success has led to a loss of authenticity and a departure from the values that once defined the sector. The conversation about clothing thus becomes a proxy for broader discussions about power, responsibility, and identity in an era of rapid technological change. in the end, whether one approves or disapproves, the scrutiny of tech executives' wardrobes shows no sign of fading in the foreseeable future. In an age where image is constantly curated and shared across social media platforms, the line between personal choice and public expectation remains blurred and increasingly difficult to define. What matters most, perhaps, is that the attention does not overshadow the real issues that technology companies and their leaders must address.

long_sentences.en: As Emma Childs wonderfully observed in The Cut, “a $9,000 leather moto is not the outerwear of a man faithfully going home to his wife and kids after a long day of architecting the AI revolution.” And since Huang’s tomfoolery has managed to spank more than $1 trillion in less than a month, something has to be done.

The message needs to be ‘I’m a serious person, and I’m leaving that tragic try-hard boomer dad wardrobe behind along with my despicable behavior.’” Clarkson agrees, saying that while the term “unapologetic” is often used in fashion, in this instance, Huang needs a more apologetic dress code, moving away from anything too flashy.

So out go the overtly sexual Tom Ford leathers—which Jensen can handily sell off for $1 million a pop to his Huang-boys to offset any alimony outlays that may, or may not, be coming his way—and in come understated and neutral tones.
